extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians and computer scientists who write or teach proofs (including authors of algorithm correctness proofs)
extracted.subtask_description: Applying Leslie Lamport's '21st Century Proof' methodology: introduce hierarchical structure, explicit scoping and naming, and TLA+/formal tools to make mathematical and algorithmic proofs clearer, less error-prone, and checkable. Includes practical steps for rewriting informal prose proofs into structured proofs and pedagogical advice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use structured proofs (Lamport's approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt a structured proof style (hierarchical steps, explicit roles for statements) rather than informal continuous prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structured proofs introduce rigor in structure and naming, making it possible to avoid errors (though not guaranteeing it). Start by adding structure to an existing proof, rewriting simple proofs first and then longer ones. The approach is particularly useful for proofs longer than about ten lines and for algorithm correctness proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduce explicit structure and naming
rubrics_metrics.description: Use structure to formally identify the roles of statements and naming to make it clear which facts are being used and referred to.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Naming clarifies which facts are used and referred to; structural markers show how statements connect. This reduces ambiguity and helps reveal unstated preconditions or missing hypotheses that can cause errors in algorithms or mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: ASSUME / PROVE and NEW
rubrics_metrics.description: Use ASSUME to state the set of facts 'in scope' for a subsequent proof, PROVE to show the goal of that step, and NEW to introduce a new variable with conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These statements provide explicit scoping: NEW introduces a variable and its conditions; ASSUME limits what is available in the current scope; PROVE makes the goal explicit. Follow the TLA+ usage as a model.

rubrics_metrics.name: SUFFICES A
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'SUFFICES A' to assert that proving A suffices to prove the current goal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This lets you replace the current goal with a different proposition that implies it, making the proof structure clearer. See TLA+ guide (p25) for more detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: PICK (introduce witnesses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use PICK to introduce a new variable by asserting 'pick some x in S' and requiring the proof to show the asserted statement about that x.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PICK both introduces the variable and asserts the existence/property that must be proved, making existential steps explicit and scoped correctly.

rubrics_metrics.name: CASE for case-by-case reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Use CASE to structure reasoning that proceeds by cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure each case as its own scoped subproof so assumptions in one case cannot be (illegally) referenced in another. CASE integrates naturally into hierarchical proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hierarchical numbering and scoping to prevent illegal references
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt a careful hierarchical numbering scheme designed to prevent 'illegal' references to sub-proofs which were proved under different assumptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Think of variable scoping rules: numbering and hierarchy make clear which assumptions and variables are in scope for each subproof, preventing mistakes where a subproof's result is referenced outside its valid scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place proof sketches between statement and proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Use proof sketches between a statement and its detailed proof to summarize intent and method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof sketches can be used at any level of the hierarchy, including before the top-level proof. They allow readers uninterested in details to understand the high-level argument and skip deeper steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid distracting comments in arbitrary places
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not insert comments in arbitrary places within a proof; they can be distracting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instead, use focused proof sketches where appropriate. Keep in-line commentary minimal so it does not interrupt the logical flow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be ruthlessly suspicious; question every assertion
rubrics_metrics.description: When writing a proof, adopt the mindset that the theorem may be false and check every assertion; imagine a curious child asking 'Why?' for each step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This psychological discipline helps find gaps and missing hypotheses that confirmatory bias would overlook. Treat every assertion as something that must be justified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make implicit assumptions and prerequisites explicit
rubrics_metrics.description: Reveal unstated implications and prerequisites in informal proofs by rewriting them in structured form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Lamport-style rewrite of a Spivak proof shows how informal/illogical textbook proofs hide assumptions students are expected to infer; structured proofs force you to state them explicitly, improving correctness and pedagogy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use hierarchical structure to manage complexity (esp. algorithms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ hierarchical structuring to handle complexity in algorithm proofs, which are often mathematically shallow but detail-heavy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Traditional prose makes it hard to ensure no detail was forgotten; hierarchical structure isolates pieces, clarifies dependencies, and makes checking feasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use formal tools (TLA+ / TLAPS) where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider using TLA+ and the TLA+ Proof System (TLAPS) to formalize and mechanically check parts of proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While Lamport emphasizes methodology rather than full automation, TLAPS can automate checking of some TLA+ proofs. Formalizing proofs teaches students what a proof is and can help transition from formal to structured informal proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incremental rewriting and pedagogy
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin adopting structured proofs by incrementally reworking simple proofs and then progressing to longer ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This incremental approach is practical for adoption and teaching: rewrite a simple proof first, then try longer examples. Learning structured formal proofs helps students understand proofs better and makes the step to structured informal proofs natural.
